documents.abstract: As generative AI (GenAI) tools become accessible, their integration into K–12 writing presents opportunities and challenges. This study partnered with 21 primary school teachers in a participatory co-design process to develop StoryBot, a teacher-configurable GenAI story-authoring platform. Teachers identified instructional needs and learning outcomes that informed system features, including genre-specific writing scaffolds, configurable prompts, and constraints on full-text generation to preserve student voice. The platform positions educators as co-designers of AI behavior rather than passive users. We conducted a pilot writing workshop with 13 youth (ages 8–12) and a focus group with six educators to examine how the platform influenced students’ writing behaviors and classroom integration. Findings demonstrate the value of teacher co-design and configurable AI systems in aligning GenAI tools with pedagogical priorities and practices. We present design implications for teacher-configurable GenAI writing systems that support student agency, ethical safeguards, and instructional alignment in human–AI coauthoring environments.

This chapter examines Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based embedded perception for real-time Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) for trustworthy electric ride-hailing services. It reviews recent perception approaches for road-scene understanding, including lightweight convolutional models, You Only Look Once (YOLO)-based detectors, compact vision transformers, low-light perception, radar-aware methods, and multimodal fusion. Particular attention is given to safety-critical road elements such as pedestrians, vehicles, cyclists, obstacles, traffic signs, and traffic lights, because they directly influence driver awareness, decision-making, and perceived safety. The chapter proposes a methodological framework covering dataset selection, ADAS task definition, data preparation, model selection, AI optimization methods, embedded deployment, and evaluation. By linking perception reliability with perceived safety, user trust, and behavioral intention, the chapter positions embedded ADAS perception as a key contributor to the adoption of electric ride-hailing services.

Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is spreading through health care, yet systems that administer assessments directly to clients remain untested in occupational therapy (OT), where the initial assessment both gathers data and builds therapeutic rapport. Objective To compare user experience of a purpose-built, remote AI-administered OT initial assessment with a human-administered assessment. Methods Thirty adults completed an AI-administered and a human-administered OT initial assessment in randomized order one to two weeks apart (crossover design), rating usability, perceived compassion, goal setting and satisfaction after each and stating an overall preference; 28 gave reflection interviews. Formats were compared within participants (Wilcoxon signed-rank, McNemar, Holm-corrected) and interviews analyzed thematically. Results Participants were randomized 15 per sequence; order affected no outcome. AI usability was high (modified System Usability Scale 81.1). Perceived compassion favored the human format (median 9.90 vs 7.53; Hodges–Lehmann difference 2.39, 95% CI 1.56–3.11; p < 0.001), as did satisfaction (all p < 0.001). Agreement that goals were clear, personalized, relevant, attainable and motivating did not differ (all p ≥ 0.25), but strong agreement was more frequent after the human format on four of five items (40.0–53.3 percentage points, all p ≤ 0.002). Overall, 83% (25/30) preferred the human format. Four themes were identified. Conclusions The AI-administered assessment was highly usable and produced goals accepted as clear, relevant and attainable at rates matching the human format; what differed was the depth of endorsement, perceived compassion and preference. Conversational AI appears better placed to supplement therapist-led assessment than to replace it.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a new participant in everyday and educational communication. Learners now talk to chatbots, use machine translation and receive automated feedback on their writing. This conceptual paper examines how these tools affect the development of sociolinguistic thinking, understood as the ability to select, interpret and adapt language forms according to social context, participants and communicative goals. Drawing on sociocultural theory, social learning theory, sociolinguistics and intercultural pedagogy, the paper outlines the cognitive, social and emotional mechanisms involved and analyzes the opportunities and risks of AI as a language model and interlocutor. It then proposes five pedagogical conditions for developing sociolinguistic thinking in AI-supported learning environments: critical AI literacy, contextualized task design, teacher mediation, comparison of human and machine language, and a supportive psychological climate.

This study describes the development and realization of an intelligent plastic waste sorting system that combines computer vision, robotic control, and a graphical user interface (GUI) for real-time monitoring. The system integrates the You Only Look Once version 8 (YOLOv8) deep learning architecture to detect and classify seven distinct plastic types: polyethylene terephthalate (PET), high-density polyethylene (HDPE), single-use plastics, single-layer plastics, multi-layer plastics, squeeze tubes, and ultra-high-temperature (UHT) boxes. Sorting actions are executed by an EEZYbotARM Mk2 robotic arm, driven by an STM32F446RE microcontroller, which performs autonomous pick-and-place operations according to the recognition output. A custom interface built with Python Qt version 5 (PyQt5) enables live video visualization, delineation of detection areas, counting of identified categories, and additional functionalities such as counter reset, selective filtering, and exporting detection records to Excel. The complete setup was tested on a conveyor-based system, confirming high detection precision, dependable robotic operation, and a user-friendly supervision interface. The trained YOLOv8 model achieves a precision of 94%, recall of 95%, and mean average precision (mAP) at Intersection over Union (IoU) thresholds 0.5–0.95 of 94% across the seven plastic waste categories, confirming the effectiveness of the proposed detection pipeline. This contribution aims to mitigate the limited advancement of plastic recycling technologies in developing regions, offering a cost-effective and practical framework for enhancing plastic waste management.

STEM education is a national priority in Malaysia; however, clear gaps in learning outcomes and student participation remain, particularly in rural areas. In Sabah, very low Indeks STEM Murid (ISM) scores, coupled with declining enrolment in the STEM Package A stream, indicate persistent challenges in the quality and continuity of STEM learning at the lower secondary level. These trends suggest that many students do not experience STEM learning as sufficiently meaningful or structured to build confidence and sustain their interest in STEM pathways. This paper reports Phase 1A of a Design and Development Research (DDR) study, focusing on the needs analysis and conceptualisation of EDP.AI, an AI-assisted module designed to scaffold the Engineering Design Process (EDP) for lower secondary students in rural Sabah. Document analysis was conducted to examine challenges related to STEM learning, EDP implementation, artificial intelligence in education, and Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) in low-resource contexts. The evidence was synthesised using design rationale mapping to translate theoretical and contextual insights into actionable design decisions. The outcomes of Phase 1A include the identification of key needs and challenges, the formulation of preliminary design requirements and design principles, and the development of a conceptual model to guide the design of EDP.AI. The proposed module emphasises step-by-step scaffolding aligned with EDP stages, reduced cognitive load, low-bandwidth accessibility, and support for both student reasoning and teacher workload. Overall, this study provides a theoretical and contextual foundation for the subsequent development and expert validation of EDP.AI to support more meaningful and sustainable STEM learning experiences in rural schools.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Jailbreak attacks against large language models (LLMs) are evaluated using attack success rate (ASR), which depends on correctly identifying responses that fulfill prohibited requests. Existing evaluators can mistake refusals or topically related responses for successful attacks. We show that changing only the judge LLM can alter reported ASR by up to $82$ percentage points. We introduce the semantic reconstruction game, a training-free evaluator that decomposes compliance judgments into constrained semantic comparisons. Given only a response, an LLM reconstructs the request answered by its substantive content, excluding information merely repeated or refused. The game compares this reconstruction against similar decoy requests to determine whether it matches the original request, allowing abstention when neither candidate matches. Across three off-the-shelf LLM judges, the game achieves the lowest mean error against human labels among evaluated methods and reduces variation in reported ASR. It prioritizes avoiding false positives, even at the cost of missing some successful jailbreaks.

As gig workers receive inadequate support from digital labor platforms and (inter)national institutions, many face systemic challenges—such as income insecurity, algorithmic management, and social isolation—and turn to online communities instead. Identification with such shared spaces is fundamental to fostering relational connections and collective practices that help workers cope and succeed. However, these spaces remain poorly understood. This study examines how social media affordances and gig work type shape what social identity scholars call a “common voice” (i.e., the collective expression of identification in an online community). Using computational sentiment analysis and quantitative content analysis of 8,319 posts and 153,440 comments from six of the largest Reddit communities for gig workers, the study finds that common voices emerge, despite the atomizing characteristics of gig work (e.g., geographic dispersion and platform mediation) and the constraint of social cues on the platform that hosts the community. Moreover, common voices significantly differ between platform-specific communities and generic communities for gig workers in themes, sentiments, message length and image use. These findings extend scholarship on gig work, identification, and social media affordances by highlighting their intersection—showing how gig worker communities can act as digital collectives that foster identification and work relationships.

The rapid advancement of digital technologies, including the internet, social media, e-commerce platforms, online marketplaces, and artificial intelligence-based applications, has fundamentally transformed consumer behavior in the digital marketplace. Consumers are no longer passive recipients of marketing messages; instead, they actively seek information, evaluate alternatives, engage with brands, and make purchasing decisions through various digital channels. This transformation has led to the emergence of Digital Consumer Behavior as a critical determinant of marketing effectiveness and business sustainability in the digital economy. This study aims to examine the influence of Digital Consumer Behavior on Consumer Trust and Purchase Decision, as well as to investigate the mediating role of Consumer Trust in this relationship. A quantitative research approach was employed using a survey method involving 100 active digital platform users who had conducted online purchases within the previous six months. Respondents were selected through purposive sampling, and data were analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling–Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS). The empirical findings reveal that Digital Consumer Behavior has a positive and significant effect on Consumer Trust and Purchase Decision. Furthermore, Consumer Trust significantly influences Purchase Decision. The mediation analysis demonstrates that Consumer Trust significantly mediates the relationship between Digital Consumer Behavior and Purchase Decision. The coefficient of determination indicates that the model explains of the variance in Consumer Trust of the variance in Purchase Decision having a strong relationship. These findings provide theoretical support for the integration of digital consumer behavior and consumer trust perspectives within contemporary marketing literature. From a managerial perspective, businesses should focus on delivering informative, interactive, and trustworthy digital experiences to strengthen consumer trust and enhance purchasing decisions. The study concludes that technological advancements have significantly reshaped how consumers acquire information, build trust, evaluate product alternatives, and make purchasing decisions in a faster, more efficient, and increasingly rational manner.

This research note reconsiders the conceptualisation of innovation in the era of generative artificial intelligence (AI). Based on observations from an academic writing course, this research identifies a pattern of excessive textual production with limited intellectual gain. The note interprets this phenomenon as digital involution, in which generative AI lowers the cost of output yet intensifies empty competition among students. The underlying logic aligns with theories of symbolic capital, performativity and algorithmic scale, suggesting that the efficiency of generative AI may increase peer pressure toward quantifiable output at the expense of substantive learning. Rather than defining innovation through productivity and efficiency, this note argues that AI-assisted writing risks a degenerated form of competition through the accelerated production of inflated content and reduced cognitive engagement. The research calls for redesigned assessment and pedagogical practices grounded in the Literacy of Refusal. Future study should prioritise meaningful learning outcomes and the development of critical thinking over textual expansion in AI-assisted environments.

Digital pathology, driven by whole-slide imaging (WSI), digital slide management, and computational image analysis, is increasingly transforming veterinary diagnostic pathology. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning and deep learning, provides opportunities to automate or assist tasks such as lesion detection, tissue segmentation, mitotic figure identification, immunohistochemistry quantification, and morphometric analysis. However, successful implementation requires more than scanner acquisition or algorithm development. This chapter presents a practice-oriented overview of digital pathology and AI in veterinary diagnostic pathology, emphasizing the complete workflow from tissue processing and slide preparation to scanning, digital viewing, reporting, validation, and quality management. Major pre-analytic, analytic, and post-analytic sources of error are discussed, together with principles for validating whole-slide imaging for primary diagnosis and maintaining ongoing quality assurance. The chapter also describes major AI task types, annotation and ground-truth challenges, performance evaluation, external validation, model monitoring, and responsible deployment. Particular attention is given to veterinary-specific challenges, including species and breed heterogeneity, stain variability, domain shift, limited annotated datasets, data governance, and automation bias. Emerging approaches such as foundation models, self-supervised learning, multimodal integration, and federated learning are also considered. Overall, effective digital pathology adoption depends on rigorous validation, continuous quality management, appropriate interpretation, and pathologist-led diagnostic accountability. Keywords Keywords: Digital pathology; whole-slide imaging; artificial intelligence; computational pathology; veterinary diagnostic pathology; machine learning;

documents.abstract: Rapid urbanization has intensified congestion, pollution, and inefficiencies in transportation systems, necessitating sustainable and intelligent mobility solutions. Smart mobility has emerged as a transformative approach driven by digital transformation and advanced technologies. This chapter examines the role of the Internet of Things (IoT), Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), Big Data Analytics, and Cloud Computing in enhancing operational efficiency, real-time decision-making, and service integration. It conceptualizes smart mobility through Mobility-as-a-Service (MaaS), enabling seamless coordination among stakeholders. Drawing on global and Indian examples, the chapter highlights the impact of digital platforms and electric mobility. It also addresses challenges such as infrastructure limitations, regulatory complexity, data privacy, and the digital divide. Finally, it proposes a framework for sustainable, efficient, and user-centric smart mobility systems.

Saudi Arabia’s insurance sector is expanding while simultaneously undergoing regulatory, technological and organizational transformation. Under Vision 2030, digital infrastructure, data and artificial intelligence have become explicit enablers of insurance-sector development, creating a strong policy context for redesigning underwriting. This paper examines how digital transformation can improve risk selection, pricing adequacy and operational efficiency in Saudi insurance underwriting while preserving governance, fairness and professional accountability. An integrative review approach is used to synthesize recent peer-reviewed insurance, artificial-intelligence and financial-technology literature with official Saudi policy and market evidence. The analysis identifies five mutually dependent transformation capabilities: integrated and high-quality data, advanced analytics and artificial intelligence, digitally orchestrated workflows, model governance and explainability, and underwriting talent capable of combining actuarial judgment with digital tools. The paper argues that the greatest value does not arise from replacing underwriters, but from redesigning underwriting as a human-in-the-loop decision system in which routine cases can be automated, complex risks are escalated, and pricing decisions are supported by transparent analytics. Saudi market evidence demonstrates rapid premium growth and an increasingly explicit regulatory focus on technology, data and artificial intelligence. However, implementation risks include fragmented data, algorithmic bias, privacy and cybersecurity concerns, legacy-system integration, model drift and inadequate change management. A Saudi Underwriting Digital Transformation Framework is therefore proposed, linking digital foundations, analytics, workflow redesign, governance safeguards and measurable performance outcomes. The framework provides a research and managerial agenda for insurers seeking to improve technical profitability, customer responsiveness and market resilience while aligning digital underwriting with the objectives of Vision 2030.

Within the framework of the European Erasmus+ STIAEM project, the authors of this study deconstruct the assumed homogeneity of “digital natives” regarding generative artificial intelligence adoption. Utilizing a sample of 2,052 secondary school students, the research architecture applies confirmatory factor analysis, extended Bayesian information criterion graphical least absolute shrinkage and selection operator network analysis, and latent profile analysis. Results identify distinct student profiles based on engagement and familiarity, revealing a profound relational decoupling between technological motivation and situated ethical choices. Under academic deadline pressures, nearly all (92.74%) of the sample participants succumbed to automation bias, uncritically accepting machine hallucinations. This behavioral paradox demonstrates that superficial digital fluency masks severe deficits in epistemic validation and independent thought. Consequently, in this paper the authors argue for shifting from product to process evaluation and integrating explicit algor-ethics interventions within school curricula to develop reflexive, human-centric algorithmic citizenship.

Existing research shows that generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) increases instructional design efficiency. However, there are concerns about pedagogical quality, accuracy and content bias. While prior studies address student passivity in evaluating AI content, the potential for designers to be passive in creating instructional materials remains largely unexplored. This article addresses design safeguards for AI-assisted course and learning-material development through two complementary tools: the Discernment Map, an evaluation checkpoint for instructional designers, and a set of design heuristics. The study is conceptual and design-oriented: both tools were drafted from the literature on AI fluency, automation bias and schema theory, and then refined through structured consultations with six experienced instructional designers in higher education. Though yet to be empirically validated, the practice-informed tools work at two levels: the Map operationalises human oversight of AI outputs across Product, Process and Performance dimensions for each AI-generated artefact, while the heuristics extend discernment into the design of the learning experience itself, so that learners must evaluate rather than accept AI outputs. Both are agile micro-governance tools that integrate critical judgment directly into design workflows. The approach is intended to protect long-term instructional quality against the collective erosion that unchecked AI adoption risks, and to support intentional engagement with AI that reduces automation bias.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Code generation models are actively being used in professional and educational settings. However, the competence of large language models (LLMs) to generate algorithmically diverse code remains largely unknown. We propose the DivAlgo benchmark, a large-scale dataset constituting algorithmically diverse solutions to programming problems. We also introduce a lightweight similarity metric to enable large-scale evaluation. Our experiments across 24 modern code generation models found that uncontrolled model-generated code is significantly less diverse than human solutions (capturing ~31% of human diversity), and even the best diverse code generation strategy could achieve only ~70% of human diversity. Moreover, while it was possible to steer the models to generate solutions based on human strategies, they were unable to reproduce the diversity of the human solutions. These findings indicate the limitations of code generation models in capturing the algorithmic diversity humans exhibit, and that overexposure to model-generated code can narrow programmers' algorithmic vocabulary.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are aligned to human preferences, after pre-training and supervised fine-tuning steps. However, standard RL alignment steps such as RLHF do not focus on factuality of LLMs, hence they may generate non-factual information, which could result in unintended consequences. In response, a number of factuality alignment approaches have been proposed in the literature which claim to improve factuality of LLMs on their own benchmarks. However, these methods have not been reproduced independently and are also not comparable since each uses a different base model, training data, evaluation set, judge, and metric. In this paper, we present the first independent reproduction of five factuality alignment methods, which span on-policy RL (PPO, GRPO, and Dr.~GRPO) and offline preference optimization (DPO and KTO), and compare them on a common benchmark with common evaluation metrics. We found that none of these methods reproduces in full, and on the common benchmark none of the methods significantly outperforms the base model. On closer inspection, the rewards optimize for format, length, or brevity rather than factuality and relevance, whereas the choice between on-policy and offline training matters little. Furthermore, the evaluation metrics and benchmarks are also part of the problem since they do not measure relevance of text to the prompt. Since there is no ground truth associated with the prompts, the reliance on LLM judges and retrieval for verification also makes the evaluation fragile. We release our code, data, and checkpoints.

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on diverse vision-language tasks, but their computational demands limit deployment under constrained budgets, particularly on edge devices. Many works focus on Knowledge Distillation (KD) and try to transfer knowledge from powerful teacher models to students. In addition to reducing model size, visual token compression provides a complementary route to efficiency, but introduces mismatched visual token counts that complicate direct token-wise knowledge transfer. To mitigate this, we propose DVTR-KD, a knowledge distillation framework based on \textbf{D}ense \textbf{V}isual \textbf{T}oken \textbf{R}econstruction, which reconstructs the teacher's dense visual tokens from the student's compressed tokens. We reconstruct visual states after the final LLM layer and at the input to an intermediate layer identified as important for visual-information readout. At the intermediate layer, reconstruction is supervised through the teacher's response predictions rather than by direct token-wise KL or MSE matching. An auxiliary attention-readout loss complements this response-level supervision by aligning how the student and the original teacher integrate contextual information when predicting responses. Evaluations on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DVTR-KD improves the performance of token-compressed students while retaining the inference efficiency afforded by visual token compression.

Background Collaborative Reasoning (CR) is a dialogic, learner-centered instructional approach shown to promote learners’ higher-order thinking. However, existing research has paid less attention to how learners engage in CR processes and how the temporal dynamics of engagement relate to the development of individual reasoning. Aims To address this gap, this study investigated the temporal development of behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement during CR discussions and examined how evolving engagement patterns were associated with subsequent individual reasoning. Sample The participants were 29 seventh-graders from a middle school in China. The students formed four discussion groups, and each group participated in seven CR discussions. Methods The 28 discussions were video-coded for cognitive, emotional, and behavioral interactions (6868 codes). Process mining and epistemic network analysis were used to model shifts in engagement patterns. Individual reasoning was assessed through post-discussion essays. Results Engagement patterns shifted dynamically over time, moving from socially shared regulation to sustained knowledge co-construction. Groups differed in the timing and trajectory of this transition: some groups shifted earlier, whereas others engaged in prolonged regulatory exchanges. The group characterized by later transitions produced fewer basic argumentative elements but more advanced elements in their individual essays. Conclusions This study highlights dynamic engagement patterns as an important link between collaborative processes and learning outcomes and underscores the importance of understanding temporal configurations of regulation and knowledge co-construction in collaborative learning.

The continuous advancement of remote sensing technology has enabled high-resolution Earth observation; however, interpreting these expansive images using modern Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) remains a significant challenge. Unlike object-centric natural images, remote sensing imagery is fundamentally characterized by extreme target sparsity and massive spatial redundancy. Key objects of interest (e.g., ships, vehicles, scattered buildings) often occupy less than 1% of the spatial extent, surrounded by vast, target-free backgrounds. Many existing VFMs rely on uniform dense processing (e.g., Vision Transformers), while a substantial branch adopts pixel-reconstruction pre-training paradigms (e.g., Masked Autoencoders). These designs may waste substantial computational capacity on modeling redundant backgrounds and dilute the feature representations of small, sparse targets. To bridge this structural misalignment, we propose DynamicVis , a remote sensing visual foundation model explicitly tailored to spatial sparsity in high-resolution imagery, with a focus on large-scale visual pre-training and transferable spatial representations for diverse downstream perception tasks. Architecturally, DynamicVis introduces a Dynamic Region-Aware State Space Model (SSM) that bypasses uniform computation. It adaptively routes and incrementally models only task-relevant, high-salience tokens while employing a parameter-free integration for background context, drastically reducing the complexity of processing ultra-long 2D token sequences ( ∼ 100,000). Crucially, to equip the network with robust spatial-selection capabilities, we propose a novel weakly supervised Region-Level Meta-Embedding Multi-Instance Learning (MIL) pre-training paradigm. Trained on a million-scale dataset, this paradigm promotes foreground-aware regional discrimination in the latent semantic space, mitigating the semantic ambiguity of conventional pixel-reconstruction methods. Extensive evaluations across nine diverse downstream visual perception tasks reveal that DynamicVis achieves competitive performance across region-, instance-, and pixel-level remote sensing tasks, with particularly strong results in sparse-target and instance-level perception tasks (e.g., small object detection and instance segmentation). Notably, DynamicVis processes high-resolution imagery (2048 × 2048) with merely 97 ms latency and 833 MB of memory consumption without employing any acceleration techniques (approximately 6% and 3% of a base ViT, respectively), offering a favorable trade-off between computational scalability and representation accuracy for multi-granular remote sensing analysis. Source code is available at https://github.com/KyanChen/DynamicVis .

The emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming contemporary education and challenging established assumptions underlying educational theories. This study aims to examine the challenges posed by AI in the intelligence era and analyze the need for reorientation of contemporary educational theories in response to increasingly complex human–AI interactions. A qualitative systematic literature review was conducted using scholarly literature from Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, with emphasis on publications from 2019 to 2026. The literature was analyzed through thematic analysis and critical interpretive synthesis, guided by the PRISMA 2020 framework, focusing on knowledge construction, learning processes, assessment, teacher and learner agency, ethics, and educational purposes. The findings indicate that AI is reshaping education through personalized learning, adaptive instruction, automated feedback, and expanded knowledge exploration, while simultaneously creating challenges related to knowledge reliability, learner dependency, academic integrity, assessment validity, data privacy, and human agency. The review further shows that constructivism, experiential learning, social learning, connectivism, and humanistic education remain relevant but require critical reorientation to accommodate AI-mediated learning environments. The study proposes a human-centered, AI-augmented educational paradigm that integrates technological intelligence with critical thinking, learner autonomy, teacher agency, ethical reasoning, reflective judgment, and meaningful human interaction.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Recommender systems (RSs) increasingly support self-regulated learning (SRL) through personalized resources, feedback, and strategy recommendations. However, traditional content based and collaborative filtering approaches suffer from cold start problems, while machine or deep learning methods raise interpretability concerns and LLM-based recommenders require evaluation of explanation faithfulness and hallucinations. This systematic review examines SRL-oriented recommender algorithms from an algorithmic and pedagogical perspective. Six databases were searched using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, yielding 25 eligible studies published between 2020 and 2025. The review traces the evolution from traditional filtering methods to machine or deep learning and emerging LLM-based approaches. Three major challenges were identified: cold start, limited explainability, and LLM hallucinations, alongside gaps in learner system interaction and metacognitive scaffolding. Future SRL-RS research should compare algorithms under controlled data sparsity, evaluate explanation faithfulness and source curation, preserve learner agency, integrate SRL strategies across three phases, and longitudinally assess SRL skill maintenance and transfer.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: With the widespread use of the Internet and digital technologies, online health information-seeking behavior has become an important factor associated with the patient–physician relationship. This review aimed to evaluate the relationship between online health information-seeking behavior and the patient–physician relationship in light of the current literature. English-language articles published between 2016 and 2026 were identified through a search of the PubMed database, and studies related to online health information-seeking behavior, the patient–physician relationship, health literacy, trust in physicians, and artificial intelligence were examined using a narrative review approach. The findings indicate that the relationship between online health information-seeking behavior and the patient–physician relationship is associated with the reliability of health information, health and eHealth literacy, trust in physicians, patient-centered communication, and individual characteristics. Reliable online health information has been associated with higher levels of patient engagement and shared decision-making, whereas inaccurate or misleading information has been associated with higher levels of health anxiety and problems related to trust and communication. Although artificial intelligence–supported applications may contribute to patient education, physician oversight is required for their safe use. Encouraging reliable sources of health information and supporting digital health literacy by healthcare professionals may contribute to strengthening a trust-based patient–physician relationship.

Guardrail approaches that rely on reasoning-based large language models (LLM) improve safety decisions, but come with substantial inference overhead due to the explicit reasoning. We introduce LR-Guard (Latent Reasoning Guardrail), an efficient and explainable guardrail that jointly learns structured latent reasoning and on-demand reasoning reconstruction. Our method distills a frozen teacher's analysis of safe and unsafe prompt interpretations and their comparison into compact latent representations. Joint training optimizes these representations for both safety prediction and reconstruction of the teacher's explicit reasoning traces, enabling human-readable explanations without requiring intermediate text generation for every decision. Experiments show that LR-Guard outperforms its explicit-reasoning teacher in most in-domain and out-of-domain settings on safety classification and explanation extraction, while achieving a 19.4x inference speedup at batch size one. Further, reconstructed reasoning traces from the latent information exhibit high semantic similarity to the teacher's explicit reasoning.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances large language models (LLMs) by grounding responses in external documents retrieved at inference time. In federated RAG (FedRAG), documents are distributed across multiple autonomous corpora that cannot be centrally aggregated due to privacy, regulatory, or organizational constraints. A key challenge in FedRAG is query routing: selecting a subset of relevant corpora for each query without broadcasting to all participants. Existing routing approaches rely on supervised learning, requiring a uniform retrieval embedding model across corpora and costly retraining whenever the federation changes. These assumptions violate corpus autonomy and limit scalability in dynamic federated environments. We propose RAGSpot , a training-free query routing framework that enables efficient corpus selection without requiring a shared local retrieval embedding model. RAGSpot represents each corpus using compact cluster-level metadata derived from its vector index and estimates corpus relevance via query-to-cluster matching. In addition, it introduces a rank-based fusion strategy that jointly leverages document-level and corpus-level rankings to support robust aggregation across heterogeneous embedding models. Experiments with corpora from the BEIR benchmark show that RAGSpot improves retrieval accuracy over the strongest training-based router by 1.23– \(1.48\times\) in nDCG and 1.28– \(1.66\times\) in Recall, and over the strongest LLM-based router by 1.63– \(2.01\times\) in nDCG and 1.93– \(2.34\times\) in Recall, without any further training. Also, RAGSpot achieves query latency that is comparable to, or even lower than, that of SOTA methods on average.

With the rapid proliferation of electric vehicles, the safety and reliability of lithium-ion batteries have become critical concerns. Effective anomaly detection is essential for ensuring safe battery operation. However, as battery systems and operating scenarios become increasingly complex, Battery fault diagnosis and maintenance increasingly require stronger adaptability to heterogeneous operating scenarios and intelligent human–AI collaboration. Traditional fault detection and diagnosis paradigms are usually tailored to specific scenarios and predefined workflows, making them less effective in complex real-world applications. To address the scarcity of open-source battery fault report corpora and the lack of unified maintenance knowledge representation, this study investigates a descriptive text modeling approach for battery signal reports. Monitoring signals, statistical features, anomaly records, and state assessment results are transformed into structured and readable natural language descriptions, thereby constructing a language corpus for battery health diagnosis and maintenance. Based on this framework, we propose VBFDD-Agent, a vehicle battery fault detection and diagnosis agent for automotive-grade battery systems. VBFDD-Agent integrates descriptive battery-state texts, historical case retrieval, local maintenance manuals, and large language model reasoning to generate structured diagnostic results and maintenance recommendations. Experimental results show that the proposed framework can accurately perform anomaly monitoring and provide flexible, efficient, and actionable maintenance suggestions. Expert evaluation further confirms the practical value of the generated recommendations.

Nephrology nursing has evolved significantly over the past decades, transitioning from task-oriented care to a comprehensive, patient-centered specialty that integrates clinical expertise, advanced technology, and chronic disease management.This review explores the emerging roles of nephrology nurses in the current healthcare landscape and envisions future directions shaped by technological advancements, healthcare reforms, and evolving patient needs.Current roles encompass not only hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis care but also kidney transplantation, conservative kidney management, patient education, and multidisciplinary collaboration.The increasing prevalence of chronic kidney disease and the complexity of renal replacement therapies demand advanced competencies, including leadership, research, and quality improvement.Future roles are anticipated to expand into telehealth, remote patient monitoring, artificial intelligence-assisted care, genomics-informed nursing, and community-based kidney health promotion.The integration of advanced practice nursing and nurseled clinics is expected to further strengthen chronic disease management and reduce hospital readmissions.This review highlights the need for continuous professional development, specialized training programs, and policy support to equip nephrology nurses for these evolving responsibilities.Emerging nephrology nursing roles are critical to addressing the global burden of kidney disease and enhancing the quality, accessibility, and sustainability of kidney care delivery.

High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) is one of the most widely employed analytical techniques for the qualitative and quantitative determination of compounds. Despite its exceptional sensitivity and reliability, conventional HPLC method development and data interpretation often require extensive experimental optimization, expert knowledge, and considerable time. Furthermore, peak detection, integration, and identification in chromatograms can be automated by artificial intelligence (AI) methods like machine learning and deep learning, allowing for quicker and more precise analysis of complicated datasets, resulting in the identification of compounds and the comprehension of complex reactions more quickly and creatively. From an economic perspective, these developments promote sustainable analytical chemistry and effective resource recovery. Moreover, AI can increase productivity and reduce the possibility of human error by automating chromatographic analysis. Additionally, AI has played a key role in enhanced analysis of complicated spectra in fields like spectroscopy and chromatography, as well as in handling heterogeneous data. This mini review discusses recent advancements in artificial intelligence and machine learning (ML) that enable scientists to address complex analytical challenges more effectively. It highlights the growing application of these technologies in chromatographic predictions, particularly in liquid chromatography method development. The present review further examines key AI-driven areas, including automated method development, retention time prediction, peak deconvolution, predictive maintenance, and intelligent data processing.

Rapid advances in artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) have significantly promoted using text-to-image (T2I) models to generate images with specific affective intentions. However, the emotional effects conveyed by generated images frequently deviate from target expectations, and it remains unclear whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can reliably interpret the emotion of AI-generated visual content. Existing affective benchmarks are predominantly built on natural images, while affective studies of generated images have largely focused on emotions expressed in portraits, lacking a unified benchmark for studying the emotions expressed and evoked by generated images. We therefore introduce EmoGenie, a benchmark of emotion for AI-generated images that evaluates capabilities in T2I generation and MLLM understanding across expressed and evoked emotions. It comprises 6,400 images generated by eight T2I models using 800 emotion-targeted prompts, annotated with question-answer (QA) pairs, termed EmoGenie-QA, and continuous human ratings, termed EmoGenie-Assess. EmoGenie-QA contains 90,000 closed-set questions in single-image and image-pair settings, as well as 1,057 open-ended questions for emotion description. EmoGenie-Assess benchmarks continuous affective and aesthetic prediction using 13,175 mean opinion scores (MOSs) aggregated from human ratings in terms of valence, arousal, dominance, and aesthetic quality. We further develop EmoProbe, which combines emotion question answering with response-aligned, dimension-specific regression heads for continuous score prediction. Experimental results show that EmoProbe achieves superior results on emotion-related QA tasks, while its affective and aesthetic predictions correlate better with human ratings, demonstrating its state-of-the-art capabilities of unified coarse-to-fine affective understanding for AI-generated images.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

documents.abstract: Introduction Generative AI legal assistants rely on users to describe events, evidence, and transaction histories, yet the same accounts may contain private information that is unnecessary for legal guidance. Empathetic language may affect how selectively users decide what to provide. Methods A one-factor between-subjects online survey experiment on Wenjuanxing randomly assigned 360 participants to rational, mildly empathetic, or highly empathetic AI legal responses (n = 120 per condition). Participants completed 1-5 Likert-type measures of parasocial response, privacy boundary judgment, and over-disclosure intention, together with related relational measures, and then answered an open-ended disclosure task. Results The empathy manipulation was successful, F (2,357) = 524.170, p < 0.001, and η 2 = 0.746. Stronger empathetic responses increased parasocial response (η 2 = 0.428), reduced privacy boundary judgment (η 2 = 0.242), and increased over-disclosure intention (η 2 = 0.406). The coded non-essential disclosure score rose from 0.994 in the rational condition to 6.132 in the highly empathetic condition, F (2,357) = 170.795, p < 0.001, and η 2 = 0.489. Necessary case facts remained stable, F (2,357) = 0.245, p = 0.783. Bootstrap analysis yielded an indirect effect through parasocial response of 0.214, 95% CI [0.151, 0.283], and a sequential indirect effect through parasocial response and privacy boundary judgment of 0.063, 95% CI [0.033, 0.098]. Discussion Within this consumer-dispute scenario, stronger empathetic cues reduced users' selectivity about which information was appropriate to provide. Data-minimization prompts and evidence-oriented questioning may help retain limited emotional support without encouraging unnecessary disclosure.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for human mobility generation by modeling individual routines, activities, and mobility preferences. However, existing approaches remain largely resident-centric: generating realistic individual trajectories does not necessarily recover the encounters that emerge when multiple residents co-occur at the same place and time. To this end, we study encounter-aware human mobility generation, which jointly preserves individual mobility and population-level interaction structure. We propose EncounterMob, an encounter-driven LLM framework consisting of a coarse-to-fine Encounter Generator and an Iterative Coupling Framework. The Encounter Generator first captures city-level encounter rhythms and then instantiates participant-time-venue encounters, while the Iterative Coupling Framework coordinates these encounters with personal mobility behavior through successive refinement. We further introduce an encounter recovery protocol covering encounter marginal and joint distributions over residents, times, and venues. Experiments on the Japan and NYC datasets show that EncounterMob outperforms all external baselines on all seven encounter metrics and all six personal mobility metrics. Compared with ELLMob, it reduces the participant-time-venue joint error by 40.4%/41.7% and the mean personal mobility error by 58.8%/32.7% on Japan/NYC, respectively.

Large language models are increasingly deployed without formal guarantees against toxic text generation. Existing control barrier function (CBF) based safety filters can keep the generation trajectory within a toxicity-free region, but do not enforce a positive distance from its boundary, allowing formally safe trajectories to approach the toxicity threshold arbitrarily closely and leaving little buffer against modelling errors or disturbances. We address this limitation with a Barrier Lyapunov Function (BLF) safety filter that enforces a prescribed clearance margin throughout generation while retaining the continuous-time transformer dynamics, including feedforward layers. The resulting safe input set is a half-space defined by a constraint affine in the control input, and is non-empty under certified surjectivity and classifier-nondegeneracy conditions. For margin-compatible initial conditions we prove that the clearance margin is never violated and that the prescribed clearance is restored exponentially, yielding an explicit clearance floor, and show that, as the margin vanishes, the admissible trajectories satisfy the exponential second-order CBF condition. We further derive an explicitly computable sufficient disturbance budget under which the clearance guarantee degrades gracefully. Simulations on a small transformer illustrate the resulting improvement in safety clearance.

Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-based immunotherapy has transformed cancer treatment by enabling engineered immune cells to selectively recognize and eliminate malignant targets, with CAR-T cells establishing the first major clinical success in this field. However, severe associated toxicities, logistical complexities of autologous manufacturing, and high rates of antigen-loss relapse have accelerated the development of alternative effector platforms such as CAR-NK cells. CAR-NK cells combine antigen-directed cytotoxicity with the innate antitumor functions of natural killer cells, offering a potentially safer and more readily available off-the-shelf therapeutic strategy. Nevertheless, the clinical efficacy of CAR-NK therapy is constrained by key biological and translational hurdles: brief in vivo persistence, inadequate trafficking and solid tumor infiltration, severe susceptibility to tumor microenvironment-mediated immunosuppression, and antigen escape driven by tumor heterogeneity. These biological constraints are compounded by technical bottlenecks, including cell source variability, limited large-scale expansion capacity, ex vivo functional exhaustion, and an absence of standardized manufacturing protocols. To address these multi-faceted barriers, recent advances in genome engineering, systems biology, and computational modeling provide promising routes forward. Given that prolonged exposure to immunosuppressive niches induces functional impairment, genome-editing strategies targeting inhibitory checkpoints and persistence programs are crucial; however, enhancing persistence requires stringent safeguards to mitigate toxicity risks from constitutive signaling or genomic instability. Thus, engineering next-generation CAR-NK cells necessitates balancing extended longevity, potent cytotoxicity, and safety. Multiomics approaches facilitate deeper characterization of CAR-NK functional states and tumor–immune interactions, whereas artificial intelligence–guided engineering integrates high-dimensional biological and manufacturing data to optimize receptor design, predict therapeutic performance, and accelerate translational workflows. Collectively, these innovations support a paradigm shift toward programmable CAR-NK cells that can dynamically sense, adapt, and respond to tumor evolution, driving the transition toward autonomous, highly scalable, and precisely controllable cellular immunotherapies in precision oncology.

With recent developments in Artificial Intelligence (AI), the adoption of distributed learning paradigms such as Federated Learning (FL) has emerged. In simple terms, FL enables multiple entities to collaboratively train AI models without sharing local data. The FL paradigm is particularly valuable in privacy-sensitive settings, such as financial services, because it enables institutions to collaboratively improve fraud-detection models while keeping sensitive transaction data local. However, FL schemes are prone to security vulnerabilities, where malicious clients can poison local data or model updates and degrade the global model, and hence the performance of the resulting model might be affected. Therefore, in this work, we propose Enhanced Detective, a dual-stage robust aggregation strategy that combines Median Absolute Deviation (MAD), distance-based update filtering, and FedMedian aggregation. Experiments on an imbalanced credit card dataset evaluate targeted label-flipping and weight-scaling attacks over 50 communication rounds. With 40% malicious clients, Enhanced Detective achieves an AUPRC of 0.796 and a Recall of 0.847.

Altered level of consciousness (ALOC) is among the most frequent and most consequential presentations in prehospital emergency care. Registry data from unselected ambulance populations indicate that approximately one in eight transported patients has a reduced Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score, and that even mild reductions carry substantial 30-day mortality. Assessment of consciousness governs airway management, transport destination, and activation of stroke and traumatic brain injury (TBI) pathways. The GCS and the AVPU scale (rendered AVDS in Portuguese-language services) are the instruments in routine field use, yet both were developed and validated predominantly outside the prehospital environment. This review addresses four questions: (i) the clinical importance of consciousness assessment in prehospital care; (ii) the reliability and validity of the GCS, AVPU/AVDS, and FOUR score, with specific attention to performance in EMS provider cohorts; (iii) the operational and human-factor determinants that degrade assessment accuracy in the field; and (iv) the current evidence for objective adjuncts to subjective scoring. We conducted a structured narrative review reported in accordance with the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA). PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to May 2026, combining controlled-vocabulary and free-text terms across four concept blocks: consciousness; assessment instruments; prehospital/EMS setting; and reliability, validity, accuracy, and inter-rater agreement. Records were screened independently by two reviewers. Where a prior review was identified, its reference list was hand-searched and the underlying primary studies were retrieved and cited in preference to the review, so that evidence is not double-counted. Thirty-six sources form the synthesis corpus. A narrative rather than systematic design was chosen because the eligible literature is heterogeneous in design, population, and outcome metric to a degree that precludes meaningful pooling; the trade-offs of this choice are stated explicitly. Field GCS correlates with arrival GCS ( r = 0.67; n = 12,882) and the change between the two independently predicts mortality. The GCS is the most granular instrument, but its reliability is component-dependent, with the motor component consistently weakest; after structured training, weighted kappa reached 0.85–0.96 across components, motor response remaining lowest at 75.1% agreement. For AVPU/AVDS, large prehospital datasets localise disagreement precisely to the Verbal and Pain categories: in 4.3 million paediatric EMS encounters, overall AVPU-GCS accuracy was 0.95 (kappa = 0.61) but intraclass F1 fell to 0.37 for Verbal and 0.50 for Pain, against 0.98 for Alert; in 2,900 prehospital trauma activations, GCS differed significantly between all AVPU categories except Verbal versus Pain ( p = 0.18). The FOUR score shows modestly superior reliability and validity to the GCS in ICU and ED settings but has not been validated prehospitally. Substituting GCS-motor for total GCS increases undertriage in patients over 65 ( n = 4,480,185). Automated pupillometry substantially outperforms manual pupil examination (ICC 0.99 versus 0.92), and low Neurological Pupil Index (NPi) values are consistently associated with adverse TBI outcomes, though prognostic accuracy in isolation is moderate (AUC 0.66–0.68). Ambulance-based EEG recording is feasible but remains at proof-of-concept stage. The evidence supports specific, bounded recommendations rather than broad prescription. Calibration training should target the GCS motor component and the AVPU/AVDS Verbal-Pain boundary, which are the empirically identified loci of disagreement. Total GCS should be retained over GCS-motor for field triage, particularly in older patients, and all three components should be documented and handed over alongside the total. Automated pupillometry is the most mature adjunct and warrants piloting in defined high-yield scenarios. The central evidence gap remains the principal research priority: no study has directly compared GCS, AVPU/AVDS, and FOUR score reliability within a prehospital provider cohort under field conditions.

This thesis analyzes the didactic potential of using interactive and innovative pedagogical technologies to enhance students’ learning activity, cognitive engagement, educational motivation, and participation in collaborative activities within differentiated instruction. Particular attention is paid to adapting interactive methods to differences in students’ levels of knowledge, interests, pace of learning, and individual educational needs. The role of problem-based learning, project-based learning, gamification, cooperative learning, the flipped classroom model, multimedia tools, and other innovative approaches in differentiated instruction is examined.

The data scale of energy simulation keeps increasing, particularly in urban building energy modeling (UBEM) and uncertainty analysis, where thousands of EnergyPlus runs are often required to explore complex parameter spaces and building variability. To simplify these data-intensive workflows, recent studies have introduced AI agents for end-to-end simulation tasks. However, in practice, both AI-assisted and conventional batch workflows remain constrained by unstable field inference and search bias, inefficient large-ensemble simulation execution, and cumbersome data processing. To address these problems, this study introduces Epeditor, a cloud-deployable simulation infrastructure for large-ensemble building energy analysis for both AI and human users. It combines three improvements on current workflows: a knowledge-assisted parameterization with more accurate and stable field search in IDF files; a simulator that improves parallel execution efficiency through Operating-System-Level deployment; and a data management system that enables memory-safe aggregation of large simulation inputs and outputs. The packaged Agent Skill allows AI agents to execute fully automated dataset generation, batch simulation, surrogate modeling, and interpretation through an auditable workflow. Epeditor is evaluated through a agent benchmarks with metrics for Artificial General Intelligence, and two case studies are introduced to show its ability in research and design practices including an AI-assisted surrogate-modeling case, and design-studio practices. The pipeline exhibits 99.98% robustness in IDF generation, up to four-fold acceleration in high-parallel simulation, and 76.28 ( F 1 ) in IDF field inference. These findings indicate that Epeditor can lower the technical and computational barriers to large-ensemble EnergyPlus simulation, supporting more accessible, reproducible, and AI-ready building energy analysis.

Generative AI performance disparities can exclude minority-language speakers from digital participation. Drawing on Fricker’s epistemic-injustice framework, we examined five Chinese minority languages using four-way causal mediation decomposition, intersectional analysis, and participatory evaluation. Under the measured mediators and model specification, non-PIE components accounted for an average of 67.5% of observed disparities. Tibetan speech recognition yielded a 43.9% word error rate (WER) for elderly speakers using religious and dialectal language, 6.9 percentage points above the main-effects additive reference. Community evaluation prioritized religious sensitivity, while threshold rules identified culturally salient failures missed by linear weighting. CAML-LLM, integrating cultural knowledge graphs, multimodal alignment, and community-weighted training, reduced WER from 31.2% to 22.7% and improved cultural appropriateness by 22.5%. These findings characterize model-dependent disparities and demonstrate that participatory system design can improve minority-language performance within the evaluated settings.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) in library offers a transformative opportunity to enhance service delivery amidst persistent staffing and funding deficits. However, this technological shift creates tension regarding ethical governance, data privacy, and cultural representation. This study investigated the ethical dimensions and operational usage of AI for service delivery in Nigerian academic libraries, with policy frameworks, algorithmic justice, data privacy, and technological equity. The study adopted a descriptive survey research design. The population comprised 8,323 certified librarians in Nigeria, from which a sample size of 368 was selected using a convenience/purposive sampling technique. Data collection was executed using a validated self-structured 5-point Likert scale questionnaire administered during the EDO 2025 Nigerian Library Association (NLA) Conference. A total of 318 valid copies were retrieved, yielding an 86.4% response rate. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, including frequency counts, percentages, mean, and standard deviation. The results revealed that while librarians demonstrate a high overall level of ethical awareness and a desire for structural policy frameworks (M = 3.64), their specific practical awareness regarding daily data privacy and intellectual property implications remains high (M = 3.79). Result showed that current library professional ethics are moderate (M=3.36) to regulate AI adoption. Furthermore, respondents reported a moderately critical level of algorithmic bias moderate (M=3.10), strongly indicating that current Western-centric AI systems marginalize local research, regional cultural contexts, and indigenous Nigerian languages. Concerns surrounding data privacy, cloud breaches, and third-party commercial data-mining also scored moderate (M=3.18), exposing the vulnerabilities of libraries operating with sub-baseline digital infrastructures. The study concluded that forcing AI adoption without context-responsive ethical governance exacerbates algorithmic injustice and risks compromising user trust. It is recommended that stakeholders co-design localized AI deployment policies, conduct rigorous pre-deployment algorithmic audits, and establish human-AI collaborative frameworks for patron confidentiality against aggressive data mining.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Algorithms now shape who gets diagnosed, who gets treated, and who gets overlooked, and too often they reproduce the very inequities medicine claims to fight. This chapter examines how bias enters clinical artificial intelligence and what it costs patients. Drawing on systematic reviews and real cases, it traces the mechanisms, training data that underrepresents minority populations, models that learn from unequal patterns of care, and proxies like health spending that mistake access for need, producing tools that score black patients as healthier than they are. It looks at race correction in kidney and other algorithms, uneven accuracy across racial groups in cardiovascular and imaging models, and the transparency gaps that let these flaws go unnoticed. Finally, it turns to solutions, explainable AI that lets clinicians interrogate algorithmic logic, guiding principles for fairer design, and the regulation, accountability, and physician vigilance required to ensure these systems advance justice rather than entrench disparity.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in education, but evidence on their performance comes mainly from high-resource languages. We evaluated five commercial LLMs in Kazakh in a zero-shot setting: sentiment classification on 300 class-balanced KazSAnDRA reviews and question answering (QA) on the same 300 randomly sampled KazQAD questions with and without the gold supporting passage. Exact McNemar tests with Holm correction found no significant pairwise differences on sentiment classification, one with supporting context, and nine without context under the Containment criterion. For OpenAI and Anthropic, the higher-tier model had a larger advantage over its lower-tier counterpart when the supporting passage was removed (tier-by-regime interaction: OR = 1.92, 95% CI [1.52, 2.43]). Closed-book scores were affected by output format, inflectional morphology, and answer length. Human evaluation of 500 QA responses showed that string-based metrics substantially underestimated closed-book accuracy (0.55 by human judgement versus 0.26 by Containment). Under human judgement, the three higher-scoring models did not differ significantly from one another. Access to a relevant passage narrowed differences between models, although this oracle-context condition did not test a retrieval system. These findings support task-specific evaluation of Kazakh-language educational assistants and the use of answer-matching criteria checked against human judgement.

Work on debugging LLM agents treats the "first mistake" marked by a human or LLM judge as ground truth for where a trajectory failed. We ask whether such labels point at causes or symptoms, and make the distinction executable: we restart the agent from reconstructed intermediate states of a failed trajectory and estimate its prefix value V(h_t), the probability of success from each step, with a certified point of no return (PNR) for a failure. On 150 SWE-bench Verified tasks with two frozen open-weight agents, we build such curves for 47 and 60 failed trajectories and probe every step labeled by four frontier judges under the Traverse rubric. We find that the labels do not mark what a controller needs. Judges of different lineages agree on the exact step in only 21/57 cases, and the newest judges flag mistakes in 8/10 and 10/10 successful runs. For 66% of the labels, the agent's success probability does not drop at the labeled step; only 7/188 answers name the decisive step. Restarting at the measured restart point raises expected success from 0.44 to 0.57 offline, and real restarts confirm the advantage, whereas restarting at a judge's label does not (-0.08 to -0.03). We release our code, curves, and labels.

Purpose This study aims to develop and evaluate an explainable machine-learning framework to anticipate county-level high recovery burden from natural disasters one year ahead using only public administrative and social-vulnerability data. Its substantive aim is to help built-environment decision makers shift from reactive post-event allocation to earlier, place-based prioritization of recovery and mitigation effort. Design/methodology/approach A county-year panel was assembled for 3,042 US counties over 2014–2022 by combining FEMA Disaster Declarations Summaries with county-level CDC/ATSDR social vulnerability index data. The outcome was a high-burden county-year, defined as repeated county-level declarations involving public assistance and/or hazard mitigation programme activity. Class-weighted logistic regression, random forest and XGBoost were benchmarked using a temporally ordered train-validation-test split. SHAP values and model coefficients were used to interpret predictive drivers. Findings The benchmark produced a moderate but decision-relevant predictive signal. Class-weighted logistic regression achieved the strongest out-of-sample performance on the hold-out period (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.626; area under the precision–recall curve 0.140; F1-score 0.262) and outperformed the more flexible tree-based models. Across models, stronger prior programme burden, recent major declarations, population size, mobile-home prevalence and social vulnerability were associated with higher next-year burden. Research limitations/implications The dependent variable is an administrative proxy for recovery burden rather than a direct measure of physical loss, repair cost or household recovery outcomes. The empirical setting is the USA; transfer to other countries should therefore be treated as conceptual and methodological rather than statistical. Practical implications The framework offers a transparent annual screening tool for local governments, regional planning bodies and emergency-management agencies seeking to identify counties likely to face elevated recovery pressure. Social implications Because it relies on public tabular data rather than expensive proprietary inputs, it is potentially transferable to resource-constrained settings that need interpretable anticipatory analytics. Originality/value The paper contributes a reproducible public-data pipeline that links explainable artificial intelligence to disaster-resilience planning in the built environment. It also responds to the journal’s growing interest in technology-enabled resilience by showing that interpretable models, rather than only complex algorithms, can support forward-looking preparedness and recovery prioritization.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence is one of the major technological advancements of this century, bearing incredible potential for users through AI-powered applications and tools in numerous domains. Being often black-box (i.e., its decision-making process is unintelligible), developers typically resort to eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques to interpret the behavior of AI models to produce systems that are transparent, fair, reliable, and trustworthy. However, presenting explanations to the user is not trivial and is often left as a secondary aspect of the system’s design process, leading to AI systems that are not useful to end-users. This paper presents a Systematic Literature Review on Explanation User Interfaces (XUIs) to gain a deeper understanding of the solutions and design guidelines employed in the academic literature to effectively present explanations to users. To improve the contribution and real-world impact of this survey, we also present a platform to support Human-cEnteRed developMent of Explainable user interfaceS (HERMES) and guide practitioners and scholars in the design and evaluation of XUIs.

Teenagers lack sufficient exercise and are therefore not physically fit. According to the World Health Organization, children and adolescents aged 5-17 need to be physically active in a moderate-to-vigorous way for at least 60 minutes each day. However, a survey shows that 86% of children and teenagers are in a low-active state, and the compliance rate is only 14.8%. According to the "Compulsory Education Physical Education and Health Curriculum Standards (2022 Edition)", the average heart rate of students in physical education classes should be between 140 and 160 beats per minute. Insufficient teaching load and fragmented content are still relatively common in practice. The three contents of this paper are: the quality of physical education classes, teacher support and the connection between schools and communities; the way in which these three factors affect the continuous exercise of teenagers. The results show that the classroom serves as the foundation for skill acquisition, teacher autonomy support and emotional support motivate intrinsic motivation, and the link between schools and communities provides a space for extended participation outside of class. The three factors work together and are in conjunction to promote continuous participation behaviour. In light of the problems of skill-focused teaching in teacher support and a lack of school-community cooperation, it is proposed to optimise class load and teaching organisation, promote changes in the form of teacher support, and build a regular connection mechanism between schools and communities.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely adopted in corporate innovation activities, yet prior research has not reached a consensus on whether it is more conducive to incremental or radical innovation. For radical innovation, which depends on highly novel ideas, realizing the value of AI depends not only on whether AI is adopted but, more importantly, on whether employees can use it creatively to transcend established knowledge boundaries. Drawing on environmental dynamism and the exploration–exploitation perspective, this study develops a theoretical model linking leaders’ perceptions of environmental dynamism, employees’ AI use modes, leader temporal myopia, and employee radical creativity in the context of AI-enabled drug discovery. We distinguish leaders’ perceptions of environmental dynamism into perceived technological dynamism and perceived market dynamism, and employees’ AI use into exploratory and exploitative AI use. The model is tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling and three-wave matched survey data from 368 leader–employee dyads. The results show that leader-perceived technological dynamism is positively associated with employee exploratory AI use, whereas leader-perceived market dynamism is positively associated with employee exploitative AI use. Exploratory AI use is positively associated with employee radical creativity, whereas exploitative AI use is negatively associated with it. Leader temporal myopia weakens the positive conditional indirect relationship of technological dynamism with radical creativity through exploratory AI use and strengthens the negative conditional indirect relationship of market dynamism with radical creativity through exploitative AI use. By adopting a knowledge-activity perspective, this study reveals the differentiated relationships between AI use modes and radical creativity and further explains how perceptions of the external environment, leaders’ temporal orientation, and employees’ AI use behaviors are differentially related. The findings provide a theoretical basis and practical implications for helping firms engaged in AI-enabled drug discovery guide employees toward effective AI use and enhance radical creativity.

Exploration bounds learning efficiency in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Current methods explore mostly through independent sampling, without fully using the information gathered along the way, such as known wrong answers and environment feedback. We propose LEAF, which injects a dynamic, problem-specific memory into the context before every rollout. The memory contains the most recent response, its reward, and other environment feedback. It is updated after every verifier call. We decouple policy updates from rollouts and update the policy through self-distillation. On four benchmarks and two open models, LEAF accelerates exploration by about 4x compared with a random sampling baseline. On unseen test sets, it improves accuracy over the strongest baseline by 1.59 and 1.83 percentage points on the two models, while using less compute than any RL baseline. These results highlight the potential of LEAF in improving both exploration and learning efficiency. Code is available at: https://github.com/on1262/LEAF

This article examines the extent to which private technology companies bear responsibility for respecting human rights, particularly freedom of expression, when governing social media content through artificial intelligence (AI), and how that responsibility relates to the legal obligations of States. It focuses on the rule-of-law complexities created by the interaction between territorially based public regulation and transnational platform governance. Through a comparative analysis of domestic law and platform practice, the article assesses how AI-mediated content moderation affects online expression. The revised analysis is limited to India, Bangladesh, Pakistan and Afghanistan as selected comparative cases; it distinguishes State duties from the corporate responsibility to respect human rights, and treats AI-mediated moderation as including automated detection, classification, recommendation, down-ranking, removal and account restrictions. It proposes a seven-element human-rights test for AI-mediated moderation: legality, legitimate aim, necessity, proportionality, transparency, procedural fairness and effective remedy.
